rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either the increased-shells reason or the increased-distance reason.

rubric.why: Increased shielding reduces nuclear attraction, so less energy is needed to remove an outer electron.
rubric.description: Explains that increased shielding reduces attraction to the outer electrons and lowers the energy needed to remove one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking shielding or reduced nuclear attraction to the decrease in ionization energy.

written.text: What is single covalent bond? Explain with an example.
modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.
For example, in H₂, each hydrogen atom contributes one electron and the two atoms share the pair, forming an H–H single covalent bond.
written.followUp: What is a double covalent bond? Explain with an example.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond consists of one pair of electrons shared between two atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a single covalent bond as one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two atoms share one pair of electrons.

rubric.why: A valid example identifies a molecule in which atoms share one pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Gives an appropriate example, such as H₂ or Cl₂, and identifies the shared pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example with the sharing of one pair stated.

written.text: Define intermolecular forces and give an example also.
modelAnswer: Intermolecular forces are the forces of attraction between molecules.
Hydrogen bonding between water molecules is an example.
written.followUp: What are intermolecular forces? Give one example involving water molecules.

rubric.why: The definition identifies these forces as attractions acting between molecules.
rubric.description: Defines intermolecular forces as attractive forces between molecules.

rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an intermolecular force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as hydrogen bonding between water molecules or van der Waals forces between molecules.

written.text: Why the density of gases increases on cooling?
modelAnswer: On cooling, a gas contracts and its volume decreases (at constant pressure).
Since density = mass/volume and the mass remains constant, the density increases.
written.followUp: Explain why the density of a gas increases when it is cooled.

rubric.why: Cooling makes a gas occupy less volume under the same pressure.
rubric.description: States that a gas contracts or its volume decreases on cooling.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the decrease in volume.

rubric.why: For a fixed mass, reducing volume increases density (density = mass/volume).
rubric.description: Connects the reduced volume to an increase in density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that density increases because the same mass occupies less volume.

written.text: Define allotropy and give an example also.
modelAnswer: Allotropy is the property of an element to exist in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.
written.followUp: Define allotropy and name two allotropes of carbon.

rubric.why: Allotropy is the occurrence of one element in multiple forms while in the same physical state.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an element exists in two or more different forms in the same physical state.

rubric.description: Names a correct pair of allotropes, such as diamond and graphite or oxygen and ozone.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both members of a valid allotropic pair.

written.text: How will you prove that whether given solution is a colloidal solution or not?
modelAnswer: Pass a narrow beam of light through the given solution in a dark room.
A colloidal solution scatters the light (Tyndall effect), while a true solution does not.
written.followUp: How can the Tyndall effect be used to distinguish a colloidal solution from a true solution?

rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light.
rubric.description: Describes shining a beam of light through the sample and observing scattering (the Tyndall effect).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the light-scattering test.

rubric.why: The comparison with a true solution confirms whether the sample is colloidal.
rubric.description: States that a colloid scatters the light, whereas a true solution does not.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct observation distinguishing the two.

written.text: Why benzene is insoluble in water?
modelAnswer: Benzene is non-polar, whereas water is polar.
According to the principle “like dissolves like,” polar water does not dissolve non-polar benzene.
written.followUp: Why does oil not mix with water?

rubric.why: The difference in polarity is central to why benzene and water do not mix.
rubric.description: Identifies benzene as non-polar and water as polar.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the polarity of both substances.

rubric.why: The solubility explanation applies the principle that substances with similar polarity dissolve in one another.
rubric.description: Explains that polar water does not dissolve non-polar benzene, consistent with the like-dissolves-like principle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for applying the like-dissolves-like principle or explicitly stating that water does not dissolve benzene because of their different polarity.

written.text: Define solvent and give an example also.
modelAnswer: A solvent is the substance in which a solute dissolves.
Water is the solvent in a salt solution.
written.followUp: Define a solute and give an example from salt water.

rubric.why: The definition describes the role of the solvent in a solution.
rubric.description: Defines a solvent as the substance in which the solute dissolves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: A correct example identifies a solvent in a solution.
rubric.description: Gives water as the solvent in a salt solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example.

written.text: Write two examples of weak electrolytes.
modelAnswer: Acetic acid (CH₃COOH).

rubric.description: Gives a second correct example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid example; do not award both marks for only one example.

written.text: Write two physical properties of metals.
modelAnswer: Metals are lustrous (shiny).
Metals are malleable and can be beaten into sheets.
written.followUp: Write two physical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Metals possess several characteristic physical properties.
rubric.description: Gives one physical property of metals, such as lustre, malleability, ductility, conductivity, or sonority.

rubric.why: A second distinct property is required for the full answer.
rubric.description: Gives a second distinct physical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another correct physical property.

written.text: Explain the trend of electropositivity in a group of periodic table.
modelAnswer: Electropositivity increases down a group in the periodic table.
Down the group, atomic size and shielding effect increase, so the nucleus attracts the outermost electron less strongly.
Therefore, the outermost electron is lost more easily.
written.followUp: How does atomic size change down a group, and how does this affect an atom’s tendency to lose an electron?

rubric.why: Identifies the direction of the trend.
rubric.description: Electropositivity increases down a group.
rubric.how: State the trend down the group.

rubric.why: Explains the trend using the easier loss of an outer electron.
rubric.description: Increasing atomic size and shielding reduce the attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron, so it is lost more easily.
rubric.how: Link increased size or shielding with weaker nuclear attraction and easier electron loss.

written.text: Write two uses of sodium.
modelAnswer: Sodium is used in sodium-vapour lamps for street lighting.
It is used as a coolant in nuclear reactors.
written.followUp: State two uses of sodium and briefly describe each use.

rubric.why: Gives one valid use of sodium.
rubric.description: Sodium is used in sodium-vapour lamps for street lighting.

rubric.how: Name its use as a nuclear-reactor coolant.

written.text: Write at least four differences between a compound and a mixture.
modelAnswer: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture may contain its components in any proportion.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; the components of a mixture retain their individual properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture has no fixed chemical formula.
written.followUp: Give four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: Compares the proportions of components in compounds and mixtures.
rubric.description: A compound contains elements in a fixed ratio, whereas a mixture may contain its components in any proportion.
rubric.how: Contrast the fixed ratio in a compound with the variable proportions possible in a mixture.

rubric.why: Compares the properties of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.description: A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; mixture components retain their individual properties.
rubric.how: State that compounds have changed properties while mixture components retain their properties.

rubric.why: Compares how compounds and mixtures can be separated.
rubric.description: A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Identify chemical methods for compounds and physical methods for mixtures.

rubric.why: Compares how the composition of each is represented.
rubric.description: A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture has no fixed chemical formula.
rubric.how: State that compounds have a definite formula while mixtures do not have a fixed formula.

written.text: What is dipole-dipole interaction? Explain with example of HCl.
modelAnswer: Dipole-dipole interaction is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ends of neighbouring polar molecules.
In an HCl molecule, hydrogen has a partial positive charge and chlorine has a partial negative charge: Hδ+—Clδ−.
The Hδ+ end of one HCl molecule attracts the Clδ− end of a neighbouring HCl molecule.
This intermolecular attraction between separate HCl molecules is a dipole-dipole interaction.
written.followUp: What is hydrogen bonding? Explain its occurrence between water molecules.

rubric.why: Defines the force and identifies the interacting parts of the polar molecules.
rubric.description: Dipole-dipole interaction is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ends of neighbouring polar molecules.
rubric.how: Define it as an electrostatic attraction between opposite ends of polar molecules.

rubric.why: Identifies the partial charges on the atoms in HCl.
rubric.description: In HCl, hydrogen is partially positive and chlorine is partially negative: Hδ+—Clδ−.
rubric.how: Show or state the partial positive charge on hydrogen and the partial negative charge on chlorine.

rubric.why: Applies the interaction to neighbouring HCl molecules.
rubric.description: The Hδ+ end of one HCl molecule attracts the Clδ− end of a neighbouring HCl molecule.
rubric.how: Describe the attraction between opposite ends of adjacent HCl molecules.

rubric.why: Identifies that the interaction occurs between separate molecules.
rubric.description: The attraction between separate HCl molecules is an intermolecular dipole-dipole interaction.
rubric.how: State that the interaction is intermolecular.

written.text: On what factors vapour pressure depends upon? Explain.
modelAnswer: Vapour pressure depends on the temperature and the nature of the liquid.
When temperature increases, the kinetic energy of liquid molecules increases, so more molecules escape into the vapour phase and vapour pressure rises.
The nature of a liquid affects the strength of the intermolecular forces between its molecules.
Stronger intermolecular forces make it harder for molecules to escape, giving a lower vapour pressure; weaker forces give a higher vapour pressure.
written.followUp: Explain how temperature and the nature of a liquid affect its vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of temperature.
rubric.description: Vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: State the direction of the change with increasing temperature.

rubric.why: Explains the temperature effect.
rubric.description: At higher temperature, molecules have more kinetic energy and more escape into the vapour phase.
rubric.how: Link increased temperature to greater molecular kinetic energy and evaporation.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of the liquid’s nature.
rubric.description: Vapour pressure depends on the strength of intermolecular forces in the liquid.
rubric.how: Mention the liquid’s nature or its intermolecular forces.

rubric.why: Explains how intermolecular forces affect vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Stronger intermolecular forces hold molecules more tightly and lower vapour pressure; weaker forces result in higher vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Give the correct relationship between intermolecular-force strength and vapour pressure.

written.text: Explain any four types of solution with examples.
modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at a given temperature; for example, a small amount of salt dissolved in water.
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature; for example, saturated salt solution.
A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, concentrated sugar solution.
A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, dilute sugar solution.
written.followUp: Define saturated, unsaturated, concentrated and dilute solutions, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Explains one type of solution by its capacity to dissolve more solute.
rubric.description: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at a given temperature; for example, a small amount of salt dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Define an unsaturated solution and give a suitable example.

rubric.why: Explains the solution at its solubility limit.
rubric.description: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature; for example, saturated salt solution.
rubric.how: Define a saturated solution and give a suitable example.

rubric.why: Explains a solution containing a relatively large amount of solute.
rubric.description: A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, concentrated sugar solution.
rubric.how: Define a concentrated solution and give a suitable example.

rubric.why: Explains a solution containing a relatively small amount of solute.
rubric.description: A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, dilute sugar solution.
rubric.how: Define a dilute solution and give a suitable example.

written.text: Differentiate between homogeneous and heterogeneous mixture.
modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; for example, salt solution.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, with different parts distinguishable; for example, sand and water.
written.followUp: Give one example each of a homogeneous mixture and a heterogeneous mixture, and state how they differ in composition.

rubric.description: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout.
rubric.how: State that its composition is uniform throughout.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining composition of a heterogeneous mixture and distinguishes it from a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, with different parts distinguishable.
rubric.how: State that its composition is non-uniform and, optionally, give a suitable example.

written.text: Define free radical. Give example.
modelAnswer: A free radical is an atom or group of atoms containing an unpaired electron.
Examples include Cl· and CH₃·.
written.followUp: Define a free radical and give one example.

rubric.why: A free radical is identified by the presence of an unpaired (odd) electron.
rubric.description: Defines a free radical as having an unpaired electron.

rubric.why: A suitable example completes the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as Cl· or CH₃·.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid free-radical example.

written.text: Write two properties of neutron.
modelAnswer: A neutron has no electrical charge; it is neutral.
Its mass is approximately 1 amu (1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
written.followUp: State two properties of a proton.

written.text: Why do the isotopes of an element have different atomic masses?
modelAnswer: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Since neutrons contribute to the mass of the atom, the isotopes have different atomic masses.

rubric.why: Isotopes of the same element have different numbers of neutrons.

rubric.why: The different neutron counts lead to different total atomic masses.
rubric.description: Links the neutron difference to the different atomic masses or mass numbers.

written.text: What is meant by “Dobereiner’s triads”?
modelAnswer: Dobereiner’s triads are groups of three elements with similar chemical properties.
In a triad, the atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the average of the atomic masses of the other two elements.
written.followUp: State the main idea of Dobereiner’s triads and the relationship between the atomic masses in a triad.

rubric.why: A triad is a group of three elements.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the elements have similar properties or that the middle element’s atomic mass is approximately the average of the other two.

written.text: Why shielding effect of electron makes cation formation easy?
modelAnswer: Inner-shell electrons shield the valence electrons from the attraction of the nucleus.
This reduces the effective nuclear attraction, so a valence electron is removed more easily and a cation forms readily.

rubric.why: Weaker attraction makes the valence electron easier to remove, allowing a cation to form.
rubric.description: Links reduced attraction to easier electron removal or cation formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that shielding makes electron loss or cation formation easier.

Ductility is the ability of a metal to be drawn into wires.

written.text: Describe any five characteristics of cathode rays.
modelAnswer: Cathode rays travel in straight lines and cast shadows when an object is placed in their path.
They carry a negative charge and are deflected toward the positive plate in an electric field.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances, such as zinc sulphide.

written.text: Define hydrogen bonding and explain these factors affect the physical properties.
modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is the intermolecular attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom, such as oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine, and a nearby electronegative atom.
Hydrogen bonds strengthen the attraction between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them and the boiling point is higher.
Hydrogen bonding can also raise melting point, viscosity, and surface tension.
Substances that can form hydrogen bonds with water are generally more soluble in water.

written.text: Which has more molecules: 9 gram H₂O or 9 gram sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁)?
modelAnswer: Given: m(H₂O) = 0.009 kg; M(H₂O) = 0.018 kg mol⁻¹; m(C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) = 0.009 kg; M(C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) = 0.342 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = m / M; number of molecules = n × Nₐ, where Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
For water: n = 0.009 kg / 0.018 kg mol⁻¹ = 0.50 mol.
Number of H₂O molecules = 0.50 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules.
For sugar: n = 0.009 kg / 0.342 kg mol⁻¹ = 0.0263 mol.
Number of sugar molecules = 0.0263 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ ≈ 1.58 × 10²² molecules.
Therefore, 9 g of H₂O has more molecules.

Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Biochemistry studies the substances and chemical processes of living organisms.

written.text: Define chemistry.
modelAnswer: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes it undergoes.
written.followUp: Define physics.

rubric.why: Identifies the subject matter of chemistry.
rubric.description: States that chemistry is the study of matter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying matter as the subject of chemistry.

rubric.why: Includes key aspects studied in chemistry.
rubric.description: Mentions aspects such as the composition, structure, properties or changes of matter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning at least two relevant aspects.

written.text: Define empirical formula with example.
modelAnswer: An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
For example, the empirical formula of glucose (C6H12O6) is CH2O.
written.followUp: Define molecular formula and give an example.

rubric.why: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
rubric.description: Defines an empirical formula as showing the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it gives the simplest ratio or proportion of atoms.

rubric.why: CH₂O is the empirical formula of glucose.
rubric.description: Gives a valid empirical formula example, such as CH₂O for glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a correct example.

written.text: Give two properties of positive rays.
modelAnswer: Positive rays are streams of positively charged particles.
They travel in straight lines and can pass through perforations in the cathode.
written.followUp: State two properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Positive charge is a defining property of positive rays.
rubric.description: States that positive rays consist of positively charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their positive charge.

rubric.why: Any one accepted behaviour or path is a valid second property.
rubric.description: Gives another property, such as travelling in straight lines, passing through perforations in the cathode, or being deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct additional property.

written.text: Define duplet and octet rule.
modelAnswer: The duplet rule states that an atom becomes stable when it has two electrons in its outermost shell.
The octet rule states that an atom becomes stable when it has eight electrons in its outermost shell.
written.followUp: State the octet rule and give one example of an atom that follows it.

rubric.why: The duplet rule concerns a stable outer shell containing two electrons.
rubric.description: Defines the duplet rule as attaining two electrons in the outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct two-electron definition.

rubric.why: The octet rule concerns a stable outer shell containing eight electrons.
rubric.description: Defines the octet rule as attaining eight electrons in the outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct eight-electron definition.

written.text: What is the difference between single covalent bond and double covalent bond?
modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.
A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
written.followUp: Explain the difference between a single covalent bond and a triple covalent bond.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: States that a single covalent bond consists of one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying one shared electron pair.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: States that a double covalent bond consists of two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying two shared electron pairs.

written.text: What is effusion of gases? Give an example.
modelAnswer: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole in a container.
For example, gas escaping through a pinhole in a balloon is effusion.
written.followUp: Define diffusion of gases and give an example.

rubric.why: Effusion involves gas passing through a very small opening.
rubric.description: Defines effusion as the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying escape through a tiny opening.

rubric.why: An example should illustrate gas escaping through a small opening.
rubric.description: Gives a relevant example, such as gas escaping through a pinhole in a container or balloon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example of gas escaping through a small opening.

written.text: Write the names of two allotropic forms of sulphur.
modelAnswer: The two allotropic forms of sulphur are rhombic sulphur and monoclinic sulphur.
written.followUp: Name the two crystalline allotropes of carbon.

rubric.why: Rhombic sulphur is one of the two common crystalline allotropes.
rubric.description: Names rhombic sulphur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming rhombic sulphur.

rubric.why: Monoclinic sulphur is the other common crystalline allotrope.
rubric.description: Names monoclinic sulphur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming monoclinic sulphur.

written.text: What do you mean by mass/volume %?
modelAnswer: Mass/volume percent is the number of grams of solute dissolved in 100 mL of solution.
Mass/volume % = (mass of solute in grams ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100.
written.followUp: Define volume/volume percent and write its formula.

rubric.why: The definition must identify the mass of solute in a specified volume of solution.
rubric.description: States that mass/volume percent gives the mass of solute in 100 mL of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both the mass of solute and the 100 mL (or 100 cm³) of solution.

rubric.why: The formula expresses the mass of solute per volume of solution as a percentage.
rubric.description: Gives the mass/volume percentage formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formula: mass of solute ÷ volume of solution × 100.

written.text: What are metalloids? Give two examples.
modelAnswer: Metalloids are elements that have properties intermediate between those of metals and nonmetals.
Examples include silicon (Si) and germanium (Ge).
written.followUp: What are metalloids? Give two other examples.

rubric.why: Metalloids have characteristics between those of metals and nonmetals.
rubric.description: Defines metalloids as elements with properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining idea.

rubric.why: Examples demonstrate recognition of elements classified as metalloids.
rubric.description: Gives two valid examples of metalloids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two valid examples.

written.text: Write the names of any two moderate reactive metals.
modelAnswer: Two moderately reactive metals are zinc and iron.
written.followUp: Name any two highly reactive metals.

rubric.description: Names any two moderately reactive metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each correct metal; accept other valid examples from the moderate-reactivity group.

written.text: Why is platinum used in jewellery making?
modelAnswer: Platinum is lustrous and does not corrode or tarnish easily, so jewellery made from it retains its appearance for a long time.
written.followUp: Give one reason why gold is used in jewellery.

rubric.why: Platinum is valued for jewellery because it retains its appearance and is suitable for shaping into ornaments.
rubric.description: States a relevant property of platinum that makes it suitable for jewellery.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a clear valid reason, such as its lustre, low reactivity, resistance to corrosion or tarnishing, or malleability.

written.text: Write any two chemical properties of metals.
modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides.
Some metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas.
written.followUp: Write any two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Metals undergo characteristic chemical reactions with oxygen, water, acids, or nonmetals.
rubric.description: Gives one correct chemical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid reaction or chemical property.

rubric.why: A second distinct chemical property is required.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct chemical property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid property; do not award twice for repeating the same reaction.

written.text: Write five postulates of Bohr's atomic model.
modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed circular paths called orbits or shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate or lose energy while it remains in a fixed orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between the energies of the two orbits.
written.followUp: Write any three postulates of Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy particular paths around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits or shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the electrons’ fixed orbits or shells.

rubric.why: Each permitted orbit corresponds to a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-energy idea.

rubric.why: An electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate or lose energy while in a fixed orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this postulate.

rubric.why: Electrons change orbits by absorbing or emitting energy.
rubric.description: Describes absorption for an upward transition and emission for a downward transition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing both transitions.

rubric.why: The energy exchanged is the difference between the energies of the two orbits.
rubric.description: Relates absorbed or emitted energy to the difference between orbit energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating this energy-difference relation.

written.text: Define ionic bond and ionic compounds. Also write properties of ionic compounds.
modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the transfer of electrons.
An ionic compound is a compound made up of positive and negative ions held together by ionic bonds.
Ionic compounds are usually crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because their ions can move freely.
Many ionic compounds are soluble in water and are hard but brittle.
written.followUp: Define a covalent bond and covalent compounds, then state three properties of covalent compounds.

rubric.why: An ionic bond results from electron transfer and the attraction between the ions formed.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic bond as the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complete definition.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds consist of positive and negative ions held together by ionic bonds.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic compound as a compound made of oppositely charged ions held together by ionic bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the ions and their bonding.

rubric.why: Strong attractions between ions require considerable energy to overcome.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points (or a high melting point).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Ions can move and carry charge when the compound is molten or in solution.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for conductivity with a correct condition.

rubric.why: Crystalline form, water solubility, and hardness with brittleness are characteristic properties of ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States one additional valid property of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one such property.

written.text: Write detailed note on factors affecting diffusion of liquids.
modelAnswer: Temperature: When temperature increases, liquid particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so diffusion becomes faster.
Particle size: Smaller particles diffuse faster than larger particles.
Concentration difference: A greater concentration difference (steeper concentration gradient) increases the rate of diffusion.
Nature of the liquid: Diffusion is faster in a less viscous liquid because the particles encounter less resistance.
written.followUp: Explain how temperature, particle size, and concentration difference affect the rate of diffusion in liquids.

rubric.why: Higher temperature gives particles greater kinetic energy and increases their rate of movement.
rubric.description: Explains that increasing temperature speeds up diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship and explanation.

rubric.why: Smaller particles generally move and diffuse more rapidly through a liquid.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of particle size on diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: A larger concentration difference provides a stronger gradient for net diffusion.
rubric.description: Explains that a greater concentration difference increases the rate of diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: Particles diffuse more readily through a less resistant liquid medium.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of the liquid medium, such as lower viscosity or lower density, on diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid explanation of the medium’s effect.

written.text: Differentiate between atom and ion.
modelAnswer: An atom is electrically neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
An ion is a charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons.

rubric.why: An atom is neutral because it has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
rubric.description: Atom is neutral
rubric.how: Look for the idea that an atom has no net charge.

rubric.why: An ion is charged and is formed when an atom gains or loses electrons.
rubric.description: Ion is charged due to electron gain or loss
rubric.how: Look for both the charged nature of an ion and its formation by electron gain or loss.

written.text: What is meant by electronic configuration?
modelAnswer: Electronic configuration is the arrangement or distribution of an atom’s electrons in its shells (energy levels).

rubric.why: Electronic configuration describes the arrangement or distribution of electrons.
rubric.description: Arrangement or distribution of electrons

rubric.why: The arrangement is described in terms of shells or energy levels.
rubric.description: Electrons in shells or energy levels
rubric.how: Look for shells or energy levels as the locations of the electrons.

written.text: Write two defects in Rutherford’s Atomic Model.
modelAnswer: It could not explain the stability of the atom: revolving electrons should radiate energy and eventually fall into the nucleus.
It could not explain the line spectra of atoms.
written.followUp: State two limitations of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not explain why the atom remains stable despite orbiting electrons being expected to radiate energy and fall into the nucleus.
rubric.description: Could not explain atomic stability
rubric.how: Look for the unexplained stability of the atom or the expected collapse of electrons into the nucleus.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not explain the line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Could not explain atomic spectra
rubric.how: Look for the inability to explain atomic line spectra.

written.text: Give the trend of ionization energy in periods.
modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
Nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so the outer electrons are held more strongly.
written.followUp: Describe the trend in atomic radius across a period and give a reason.

rubric.why: Ionization energy generally increases across a period from left to right.
rubric.description: Trend across a period
rubric.how: Look for an increase in ionization energy from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius make electrons harder to remove.
rubric.description: Reason for the increase
rubric.how: Look for increased nuclear attraction or a smaller atomic radius as the reason.

written.text: Define a group and a period.
modelAnswer: A group is a vertical column in the periodic table.
A period is a horizontal row in the periodic table.
written.followUp: What are a group and a period in the periodic table?

rubric.why: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table.
rubric.description: Group
rubric.how: Look for a group identified as a vertical column.

rubric.why: Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
rubric.description: Period
rubric.how: Look for a period identified as a horizontal row.

written.text: What is meant by atomic radius of atom?
modelAnswer: The atomic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the outermost shell of an atom.
written.followUp: Define covalent radius.

rubric.why: Atomic radius is a distance measured from the nucleus.
rubric.description: Distance measured from the nucleus
rubric.how: Look for the idea of a distance from the nucleus.

rubric.why: The atomic radius extends to the atom’s outermost shell.
rubric.description: Extends to the outermost shell
rubric.how: Look for the outermost or valence shell as the endpoint.

written.text: Why do atoms form chemical bonds?
modelAnswer: Atoms form chemical bonds to attain a stable electronic configuration like that of a noble gas.
They do this by completing an octet or duplet in their outermost shell.
written.followUp: Why do atoms lose, gain or share electrons when forming chemical bonds?

rubric.why: Bonding helps atoms achieve a stable outer-shell electron arrangement.
rubric.description: Achieve a stable configuration
rubric.how: Look for a stable electronic configuration, noble-gas configuration or complete outer shell.

rubric.why: A complete octet or duplet (and thus a more stable, lower-energy state) explains why atoms form bonds.
rubric.description: Octet, duplet or stability
rubric.how: Look for an octet or duplet, or the resulting stable or lower-energy state.

written.text: Why the density of a gas increases on cooling?
modelAnswer: On cooling at constant pressure, a gas contracts and its volume decreases.
For the same mass of gas, the smaller volume gives a greater density (density = mass ÷ volume).
written.followUp: Why does the density of a gas decrease when it is heated at constant pressure?

rubric.why: Cooling causes a gas to contract when the pressure is constant.
rubric.description: States that the gas volume decreases on cooling.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that cooling makes the gas contract or its volume decrease.

rubric.why: Density is mass per unit volume, so a smaller volume for the same mass means greater density.
rubric.description: Connects the decreased volume to increased density for the same mass of gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that density increases because the same mass occupies less volume.

written.text: Define dilute solutions and concentration.
modelAnswer: A dilute solution contains a small amount of solute dissolved in a relatively large amount of solvent.
Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solution.
written.followUp: Define a concentrated solution and state what concentration measures.

rubric.why: A dilute solution contains relatively little solute compared with its solvent.
rubric.description: Defines a dilute solution in terms of a small amount of solute in solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains a small amount of solute dissolved in a relatively large amount of solvent.

rubric.why: Concentration expresses the amount of solute relative to a specified amount of solution.
rubric.description: Defines concentration as the amount of solute in a given amount of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating the amount of solute to a given amount of solution.

written.text: Why is naphthalene soluble in carbon tetrachloride and not in water?
modelAnswer: Naphthalene and carbon tetrachloride are nonpolar, so naphthalene dissolves in carbon tetrachloride.
Water is polar, so it does not dissolve nonpolar naphthalene well; like dissolves like.
written.followUp: Why does iodine dissolve in hexane but not readily in water?

rubric.why: Naphthalene and carbon tetrachloride are both non-polar substances.
rubric.description: Identifies naphthalene and carbon tetrachloride as non-polar.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both substances as non-polar.

rubric.why: Polar water does not dissolve non-polar naphthalene well; substances with similar polarity tend to dissolve one another.
rubric.description: Explains why naphthalene does not dissolve well in water using polarity or the principle “like dissolves like.”
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is polar while naphthalene is non-polar, or correctly applying “like dissolves like.”

written.text: How can you justify that blood is a colloid?
modelAnswer: Blood contains particles, including cells and proteins, dispersed in plasma.
These particles remain suspended in the plasma, so blood shows the behaviour of a colloid.
written.followUp: Why is milk classified as a colloid?

rubric.why: The particles remaining suspended is characteristic of colloidal behaviour.
rubric.description: States that the dispersed particles remain suspended in the plasma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that the particles remain suspended.

written.text: Why reactivity of metals increases down the group?
modelAnswer: Down a group, the atomic size increases and the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus.
This electron is lost more easily, so the reactivity of metals increases down the group.
written.followUp: Why does the reactivity of alkali metals increase down Group 1?

rubric.why: Atoms become larger down a group, placing the outermost electron farther from the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that atomic size increases or the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus down the group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating either the increase in atomic size or the increased distance of the outermost electron.

rubric.why: The outer electron is lost more easily, so the metal reacts more readily.
rubric.description: Connects easier electron loss with increased metal reactivity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electron loss becomes easier or ionization energy decreases, resulting in greater reactivity.

written.text: Why copper is used for making electrical wires?
modelAnswer: Copper is a good conductor of electricity.
It is ductile, so it can be drawn into thin wires.
written.followUp: Why is copper used for making cooking utensils?

rubric.why: Electrical wires need a material that conducts electricity well.
rubric.description: States that copper is a good conductor of electricity.

rubric.why: A wire material must be capable of being drawn into thin strands.
rubric.description: States that copper is ductile and can be drawn into wires.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying copper’s ductility or its ability to be drawn into wires.

written.text: Why the ionization energy of Na is more than K?
modelAnswer: Na has a smaller atomic radius than K, so its outermost electron is closer to the nucleus and experiences less shielding.
The nucleus attracts this electron more strongly; therefore, more energy is required to remove it from Na than from K.
written.followUp: Why is the first ionization energy of chlorine greater than that of bromine?

rubric.why: Identifies why sodium's outer electron is more strongly held.
rubric.description: Na has a smaller atomic radius, so its outer electron is closer to the nucleus than K's.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the smaller radius or closer outer electron.

rubric.why: Connects the stronger attraction to the energy needed for ionization.
rubric.description: The stronger nuclear attraction means more energy is needed to remove Na's outer electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stronger attraction and its effect on ionization energy.

written.text: Describe the discovery and properties of neutron.
modelAnswer: In 1932, James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha particles from a radioactive source.
The beryllium emitted a highly penetrating radiation that had no charge.
When this radiation struck paraffin wax, protons were ejected from the wax; Chadwick concluded that the radiation consisted of neutrons.
A neutron has no electrical charge.
Its mass is about 1 amu, nearly equal to the mass of a proton, and it is present in the nucleus of an atom.
written.followUp: Describe how Rutherford discovered the proton and give two properties of a proton.

rubric.why: States the key experimental evidence and identification of the neutron.
rubric.description: Chadwick's 1932 experiment: alpha particles struck beryllium, and the emitted neutral radiation knocked protons from paraffin wax.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for the date/scientist, beryllium and alpha particles, and the paraffin-wax evidence.

rubric.why: Gives the neutron's defining electrical property.
rubric.description: A neutron has no electrical charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the neutron is neutral.

rubric.why: Gives the neutron's mass and location as key properties.
rubric.description: A neutron has a mass of about 1 amu, nearly equal to a proton's, and is found in the atomic nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its approximate mass and 1 mark for its location in the nucleus.

written.text: Write down four differences between molecule and molecular ion.
modelAnswer: A molecule is a group of bonded atoms with no net charge; a molecular ion is a group of bonded atoms with a net charge.
A molecule is electrically neutral, whereas a molecular ion has a positive or negative charge.
A molecule has equal numbers of protons and electrons; a molecular ion has unequal numbers of protons and electrons.
Examples: H2O is a molecule, while NH4+ is a molecular ion.
written.followUp: Write down four differences between an atom and an ion.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a molecule has no net charge.

rubric.why: Identifies the overall charge that distinguishes a molecular ion from a molecule.
rubric.description: A molecular ion has a net positive or negative charge, unlike a neutral molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a molecular ion has a net charge.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the two by their numbers of protons and electrons.
rubric.description: A molecule has equal numbers of protons and electrons; a molecular ion has unequal numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the correct proton/electron distinction for both.

rubric.why: Gives an example of each type to illustrate the distinction.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct molecule example and one correct molecular-ion example.

written.text: Define ionic bond. Explain it with an example.
modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the transfer of electrons.
For example, a sodium atom transfers its outermost electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes a positive ion, Na⁺, and chlorine becomes a negative ion, Cl⁻.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other and form the ionic compound sodium chloride, NaCl.

rubric.why: Explains the electron transfer and resulting ions in the example.
rubric.description: In sodium chloride, sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

rubric.why: Connects the ions' attraction to formation of the ionic compound.
rubric.description: The attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forms the ionic compound NaCl.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the ionic attraction producing sodium chloride.

written.text: Explain any four types of solutions with examples.
modelAnswer: A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute; for example, a small amount of sugar dissolved in water.
A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute; for example, a large amount of sugar dissolved in water.
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a solvent at a particular temperature; for example, saturated salt water.
An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature; for example, salt water to which more salt can still be added and dissolved.
written.followUp: Describe dilute, concentrated, saturated and unsaturated solutions, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Defines a dilute solution by its relatively small amount of dissolved solute.

rubric.why: Defines a concentrated solution by its relatively large amount of dissolved solute.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a saturated solution by its solubility limit at a given temperature.

written.text: Define shell and sub-shell.
modelAnswer: A shell is a main energy level around the nucleus in which electrons are present.

written.text: Define Newland's Octaves.
modelAnswer: Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing atomic masses.
He observed that the properties of every eighth element were similar to those of the first, like notes in an octave of music.

written.text: What is difference between short period and long period?
modelAnswer: Short periods (the 1st, 2nd and 3rd) contain 2 or 8 elements.

written.text: Define ionization energy and write its unit.
modelAnswer: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.

written.text: Why boiling point of water is higher than boiling point of alcohol?
modelAnswer: Water molecules form stronger and more extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds than alcohol molecules.
More energy is needed to overcome these attractions and separate the water molecules, so water has a higher boiling point.

written.text: Describe any five results of the experiment of Rutherford's atomic model.
modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without deflection, showing that most of the atom is empty space.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles.
A very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles.
About one alpha particle in 8000 rebounded, turning back through nearly 180°.
The deflections showed that nearly all the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.

written.text: Define atomic number and Mass number.

written.text: What is the difference between electron affinity and electro-negativity?
modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom.
Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a chemical bond to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself.

written.text: Give the trend of ionization energy in a period. Also give reason.
modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
Nuclear charge increases and atomic size generally decreases, so the outer electron is attracted more strongly to the nucleus and requires more energy to remove.

written.text: What is the difference between Mendeleev's Periodic law and modern periodic law?
modelAnswer: Mendeleev's periodic law states that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses.
The modern periodic law states that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

written.text: Why does a Covalent bond become Polar?
modelAnswer: A covalent bond becomes polar when the bonded atoms have different electronegativities and share the bonding electrons unequally.
This unequal sharing produces partial positive and partial negative ends in the bond.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the unequal sharing produces partial positive and negative ends because the atoms attract electrons differently.

written.text: Give any two characteristic properties of Ionic Compounds.
modelAnswer: Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points because of the strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions.

written.text: Define the term allotropy with example.
modelAnswer: Allotropy is the existence of the same element in two or more different forms in the same physical state.

written.text: What do you mean by volume/mass % ?
modelAnswer: Volume/mass percentage is the volume of solute, in mL, present in 100 g of solution.

written.text: What do mean, "like dissolves like"? Give an example.
modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that a solute dissolves best in a solvent with similar polarity: polar substances dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar substances in non-polar solvents.

written.text: Why is magnesium harder than sodium?
modelAnswer: Magnesium contributes two valence electrons per atom to the metallic bond, while sodium contributes only one.
This gives magnesium stronger metallic bonding, so magnesium is harder than sodium.

written.text: Why the ionization energy of alkaline earth metals is higher than alkali metals?
modelAnswer: In the same period, an alkaline earth metal has a greater nuclear charge and a smaller atomic radius than the alkali metal before it.
Its outer electron is therefore held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it.

written.text: Why the ionization energy of sodium is less than magnesium?
modelAnswer: Magnesium has a greater nuclear charge and a smaller atomic radius than sodium, while their outer electrons are in the same principal shell.
The outer electron in magnesium is held more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it; therefore, sodium’s ionization energy is lower.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct explanation and conclusion.

written.text: Write down any five postulates of Bohr's atomic Model?
modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed circular orbits, also called stationary orbits.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in an allowed stationary orbit.
An electron absorbs or emits energy only when it jumps between orbits; the energy change equals the difference between the two energy levels.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized: mvr = nh/2π, where n is a whole number.
written.followUp: State any five postulates of Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons can occupy only particular allowed orbits around the nucleus.

rubric.why: Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that each allowed orbit has a definite or fixed energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the energy-level postulate.

rubric.why: An electron in an allowed stationary orbit does not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: States that an electron in an allowed orbit does not radiate energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-radiation postulate.

rubric.why: Energy is exchanged during transitions between orbits, and Bohr restricted the allowed angular momentum to quantized values.
rubric.description: States the energy-transition postulate and gives the quantized angular-momentum condition.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for both the transition-and-energy statement and mvr = nh/2π, where n is a whole number.

written.text: Write down any four differences between molecule and molecular ion?
modelAnswer: A molecule is a group of chemically bonded atoms with no net electrical charge; a molecular ion is a bonded group of atoms with a net charge.
A molecule has equal numbers of protons and electrons; a molecular ion has unequal numbers of protons and electrons.
A molecule is written without an overall charge, whereas a molecular ion is written with its charge as a superscript.
Examples: H2O is a molecule; NH4+ is a molecular ion.

written.text: Define diffusion and describe the effect of any three factors on it.
modelAnswer: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
Increasing temperature increases the kinetic energy of particles, so diffusion becomes faster.

Smaller or lighter particles diffuse faster than larger or heavier particles.

written.text: Give any four characteristics of a Solution.
modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition throughout.

written.text: Define hydrogen bonding and explain it with example
modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is a relatively strong intermolecular attraction between molecules.
It occurs when hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom is attracted to a lone pair on an electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule.
In water, the partially positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the oxygen atom of a neighbouring water molecule.
This attraction between water molecules is a hydrogen bond.
written.followUp: What type of hydrogen bonding occurs between water molecules? Explain briefly.

rubric.why: Awards credit for defining hydrogen bonding as an attraction between molecules.
rubric.description: Defines hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular attraction.
rubric.how: State that it is an attraction between molecules; identifying it as a relatively strong intermolecular force also earns credit.

rubric.why: Identifies how hydrogen bonding forms.
rubric.description: Explains that hydrogen attached to a highly electronegative atom is attracted to a lone pair on another molecule.
rubric.how: Mention hydrogen bonded to an electronegative atom and attraction to a lone pair.

rubric.how: Explain that the partially positive hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the oxygen of another.

written.text: Define vapour pressure and discuss the factors affecting it
modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour above its liquid in a closed container when the liquid and vapour are in equilibrium.
Vapour pressure increases when temperature increases because more liquid molecules have enough energy to escape into the vapour.
Vapour pressure also depends on the nature of the liquid: stronger intermolecular forces hold molecules in the liquid more strongly and result in lower vapour pressure.
written.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how it is related to the vapour pressure of a liquid.

rubric.why: Credits the definition and its essential equilibrium condition.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure as the pressure exerted by a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid.
rubric.how: Mention the vapour, the liquid, and equilibrium.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure increases when temperature increases.
rubric.how: Give the direction of change as temperature rises.

rubric.why: Checks how the nature of the liquid affects vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States that stronger intermolecular forces result in lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Relate stronger forces to fewer molecules escaping into the vapour.

written.text: Calculate the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄ when O.N of H = +1 and O = -2
modelAnswer: Let the oxidation number of sulphur be x.
Since H₂SO₄ is neutral, the sum of the oxidation numbers is zero.
Therefore, the oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄ is +6.

written.text: Describe mass/mass percentage of a solute present in solution
modelAnswer: Mass/mass percentage is the mass of solute present in 100 mass units of solution.
Mass/mass percentage = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100%.
The mass of solution is the mass of solute plus the mass of solvent.

written.text: Define substance and mixture
modelAnswer: A substance is a form of pure matter with a fixed composition and characteristic properties.
A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances, in which the substances retain their properties.

written.text: Differentiate between ionic and covalent compound with one example each
modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are formed by transfer of electrons, producing oppositely charged ions; for example, sodium chloride (NaCl).
Covalent compounds are formed when atoms share electrons; for example, water (H₂O).

rubric.how: Name electron sharing and give a valid covalent example.

written.text: Derived molecular formula from empirical formula with one example
modelAnswer: The molecular formula is obtained by multiplying the empirical formula by a whole number n.
n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass.
For glucose, the empirical formula is CH₂O and its empirical formula mass is 30.
Molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆.

written.text: Write any two features of long form of periodic table

written.text: Define Hydrogen bonding
modelAnswer: A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction involving a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, usually F, O, or N.
The hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on a highly electronegative atom of the same or a neighbouring molecule.

written.text: Why is the evaporation a continuous process?
modelAnswer: Molecules in a liquid are in continuous motion, and some surface molecules always have enough kinetic energy to escape into the air.

written.text: Define solution and aqueous solution
modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent.
An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.

modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than the maximum amount that can dissolve in the solvent at a given temperature.

written.text: What is meant by co-ordinate covalent bond? Explain it with two examples
modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
In the ammonium ion, NH3 donates a lone pair from nitrogen to H+, forming NH4+: NH3 + H+ → NH4+.
In the hydronium ion, H2O donates a lone pair from oxygen to H+, forming H3O+: H2O + H+ → H3O+.

written.text: Define saturated and supersaturated solution? Also describe how supersaturated solution is prepared
modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
To prepare one, heat the solvent and dissolve extra solute until the solution is saturated at the higher temperature.
Cool the hot solution slowly and undisturbed so that the excess solute remains dissolved.

written.text: Write the postulates of Bohr's Atomic Theory.

written.text: Write any five differences between Rutherford's Atomic Theory and Bohr's theory.

written.text: What is vapour pressure? On which factors does vapour pressure depend upon?
modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour above a liquid when the vapour and liquid are in dynamic equilibrium in a closed container.
It depends on temperature: increasing the temperature increases vapour pressure.
It also depends on the nature of the liquid and the strength of its intermolecular forces.
A more volatile liquid, with weaker intermolecular forces, has a higher vapour pressure at the same temperature.

written.text: How nucleus was discovered by Rutherford?
modelAnswer: Rutherford directed a beam of alpha particles at a very thin gold foil and observed their paths on a fluorescent screen.
Most particles passed straight through, some were deflected, and a very few bounced back.
He concluded that most of an atom is empty space and that its positive charge and most of its mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.

written.text: Explain that evaporation is a continuous and cooling process.
modelAnswer: Evaporation occurs continuously from the surface of a liquid, even below its boiling point.

The energy needed for evaporation is taken from the liquid and its surroundings; therefore, evaporation is a cooling process.

written.text: How much NaOH is required to prepare its 500 cm³ of 0.4M solution.
modelAnswer: Given: C = 0.4 mol dm⁻³ = 400 mol m⁻³; V = 500 cm³ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

Formula: n = CV.
Formula: m = n × molar mass.

written.text: Explain dipole-dipole interaction with example of HCl.
modelAnswer: An HCl molecule is polar because chlorine attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen.
Thus, hydrogen has a partial positive charge (Hδ⁺) and chlorine has a partial negative charge (Clδ⁻).
The partially positive hydrogen end of one HCl molecule is attracted to the partially negative chlorine end of a neighbouring molecule.
This attraction between the opposite ends of neighbouring polar molecules is called dipole–dipole interaction.

written.text: What is molarity? Write its formula and explain how one molar solution of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is prepared?
modelAnswer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution.
M = number of moles of solute / volume of solution in dm³ (M = n/V).
Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹.
Weigh 40 g of NaOH and dissolve it in a small amount of distilled water.
Transfer the solution to a one-litre volumetric flask, add distilled water up to the mark, and mix well.

written.text: What were the defects in Rutherford's Model and also write the questions initiated by these defects?
modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom: a revolving electron should radiate energy, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus.
This raised the question: Why do electrons not lose energy and fall into the nucleus? How does an atom remain stable?
The model could not explain the line spectrum of atoms.
This raised the question of how electrons are arranged around the nucleus and whether they occupy specific orbits or energy levels.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula represents the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound; for an ionic compound, it represents the simplest ratio of ions in its formula unit.

For an ionic compound, the formula gives the simplest ratio of ions. For example, MgCl2 represents a 1:2 ratio of magnesium ions to chloride ions.

The electrons can move freely through the lattice, so metals conduct electricity.

written.text: Why does ionization energy of elements decrease from top to bottom in a group?

written.text: What are the saturated and super saturated solutions, explain with examples.
modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
For example, a sugar solution is saturated when no more sugar dissolves at that temperature.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally contain at the same temperature.
It can be prepared by dissolving extra solute in a hot saturated solution and then cooling it carefully; it is unstable and excess solute may crystallize out.

written.text: What were the postulates of Bohr’s atomic model?
modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed, permitted circular orbits called stationary orbits or energy levels.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy, and an electron does not radiate energy while it remains in that orbit.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized: mvr = nh/2pi, where n = 1, 2, 3, ...
An electron absorbs or emits energy only when it jumps between energy levels; the energy change is ΔE = hν.
The energy levels are discrete, so electrons cannot have energies between the permitted levels.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-radiation postulate.

rubric.why: The allowed energy states are separate rather than continuous.
rubric.description: States that energy levels are discrete and there are no intermediate allowed energies.

written.text: Write effect of intermolecular forces on evaporation.

written.text: Compare the Rutherford and Bohr's atomic theories.
modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus, with electrons revolving around it.
Rutherford’s model did not describe fixed energy levels for the electrons and could not explain the stability of the atom.
Bohr proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in specific fixed orbits, each having a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while in these stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when they move between energy levels.

written.text: Define vapour pressure? Explain various factors effecting it.
modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapours of a liquid when they are in equilibrium with the liquid at a particular temperature.
Temperature: On increasing temperature, more liquid particles gain enough energy to escape into the vapour phase, so vapour pressure increases.
Nature of the liquid: Liquids with weaker intermolecular forces evaporate more readily and have higher vapour pressure; stronger forces give lower vapour pressure.
Nonvolatile solute: Dissolving a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid.

written.text: Explain five postulates of Bohr's atomic model.
modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits called energy levels or shells.
An electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate or absorb energy; its energy remains constant.
Only certain orbits are allowed, and the electron’s angular momentum is quantized: mvr = nh/2π.
The energy of an orbit increases as its distance from the nucleus increases.
An electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between orbits; ΔE = hν.

written.text: Define free radical, how is it generated?

written.text: Define ionic compounds and write their three properties
modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are formed by the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
They usually have high melting points and high boiling points.
They are usually soluble in water.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

written.text: How boiling point of liquid depends on nature of liquid and intermolecular forces.
modelAnswer: The boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid and the strength of the forces between its particles.
A liquid with stronger intermolecular forces has a higher boiling point because more heat is needed to overcome those forces and separate the particles.
A liquid with weaker intermolecular forces has a lower boiling point because less heat is needed to separate its particles.

written.text: How can you differentiate between substance and mixture?

written.text: What is a coordinate covalent bond? Explain it with the help of examples.

In H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺, oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to H⁺, forming a coordinate covalent bond.

written.text: Why the bigger size atoms have more shielding effect?

written.text: Compare Rutherford’s atomic theory with Bohr’s atomic theory.
modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of its mass.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus, and most of the atom is empty space.
Rutherford’s model could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus, or explain atomic line spectra.
Bohr proposed that electrons can revolve only in certain fixed orbits or shells, each with a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while they remain in these allowed orbits.
An electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between energy levels; this explains atomic stability and the hydrogen line spectrum.
written.followUp: Describe how Bohr’s model explains the line spectrum of hydrogen.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons do not radiate energy in allowed orbits and 1 mark for stating that they absorb or emit definite energy during transitions, explaining the line spectrum or stability.

written.text: What is the Trend of Ionization Energy in a Period from Left to Right?

written.text: State Dobereiner's Triads.
modelAnswer: Dobereiner's triads are groups of three elements with similar chemical properties, arranged in order of increasing atomic mass.

written.text: Define Double Covalent Bond.
modelAnswer: A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
The shared pairs hold the two atoms together.

written.text: What is meant by Hydrogen Bond?
modelAnswer: A hydrogen bond is a weak force of attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom and another electronegative atom.

written.text: Write names of various types of Chemical Bonds.
modelAnswer: The types of chemical bonds include ionic (electrovalent), covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonds.

written.text: How Vapour Pressure is affected by Nature of Liquid?
modelAnswer: Liquids with strong intermolecular forces have low vapour pressure because fewer particles escape from the liquid surface.
Volatile liquids, with weaker intermolecular forces, have higher vapour pressure.

written.text: Define Oxidation in terms of Electron.

written.text: Explain any five branches of Chemistry.
modelAnswer: Physical chemistry studies the physical properties of matter and the changes in energy accompanying chemical reactions.
Organic chemistry is the branch that studies carbon compounds.
Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
Industrial chemistry deals with the manufacture of chemicals and other products on an industrial scale.
Nuclear chemistry studies changes in the nuclei of atoms, including radioactive processes.

written.text: Define Evaporation. How it is effected by different factors?
modelAnswer: Evaporation is the escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid into vapour; it can occur at temperatures below the liquid’s boiling point.
Increasing the temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
Increasing the exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
Increasing wind speed increases evaporation, while increasing humidity decreases it.

written.text: What is modern definition of element?
modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of atoms having the same atomic number.
Thus, all atoms of an element have the same number of protons in their nuclei.

written.text: What is relative atomic mass?
modelAnswer: Relative atomic mass is the average mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

written.text: Write down the electronic configuration of chloride ion (Cl⁻).
modelAnswer: A chlorine atom has 17 electrons and gains one electron to form Cl⁻, so the ion has 18 electrons.
Electronic configuration of Cl⁻ = 2, 8, 8 (or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶).

written.text: Why does atomic size of atom decrease from left to right?
modelAnswer: From left to right, the nuclear charge increases as the number of protons increases.
The added electrons enter the same shell, so the stronger attraction pulls them closer to the nucleus and atomic size decreases.

written.text: How many periods are considered normal period?
modelAnswer: There are two normal periods: the second and the third periods.

written.text: Write difference between bond pair of electrons and lone pair of electrons.
modelAnswer: A bond pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.
A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that is not shared in a bond.

written.text: What is meant by duet rule and octet rule?
modelAnswer: According to the duet rule, an atom tends to attain two electrons in its outermost shell.
According to the octet rule, an atom tends to attain eight electrons in its outermost shell.

written.text: Why is silver and gold less reactive?

written.text: Why is ionization energy of Na more than K?

written.text: Differentiate between Steel and Stainless steel.

written.text: How neutrons were discovered? Write any two properties of neutrons.
modelAnswer: In 1932, James Chadwick bombarded beryllium with alpha particles.
A highly penetrating neutral radiation was produced; it knocked protons out of paraffin wax, leading Chadwick to identify the neutron.
A neutron has no electric charge.
Its mass is approximately 1 amu, and it is found in the atomic nucleus.

written.text: What are isotopes ? Describe isotopes of hydrogen, carbon and chlorine.

Carbon has three common isotopes: carbon-12 (¹²₆C; 12C), carbon-13 (¹³₆C; 13C) and carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C; 14C).
Chlorine has two common isotopes: chlorine-35 (³⁵₁₇Cl; 35Cl) and chlorine-37 (³⁷₁₇Cl; 37Cl).

written.text: How is a coordinate covalent bond formed ? Explain with two examples.
modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons of a shared pair to another atom or ion.
The donated pair is usually a lone pair.
In ammonia, nitrogen donates a lone pair to H+: NH3 + H+ → NH4+; the coordinate bond is shown by N→H.
In water, oxygen donates a lone pair to H+: H2O + H+ → H3O+; the coordinate bond is shown by O→H.
The atom donating the lone pair is the donor, and the atom accepting it is the acceptor.

written.text: Calculate the number of moles and number of molecules present in 6 grams of water.

written.text: Define covalent compounds and write their four properties.
modelAnswer: Covalent compounds are compounds in which atoms are held together by sharing one or more pairs of electrons.
They generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.
They are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
Many are gases or liquids, or are soft solids, at room temperature.
written.followUp: Define ionic compounds and write four of their properties.

rubric.why: Covalent bonding is based on sharing electron pairs.
rubric.description: Defines covalent compounds as compounds whose atoms are bonded by sharing electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition that includes sharing of electrons between atoms.

rubric.why: Many simple covalent compounds have relatively weak forces between their molecules.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the low melting/boiling point property.

rubric.why: They generally do not have mobile charged particles to carry current.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds are poor conductors or do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electrical conductivity property.

rubric.description: States that they are generally insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the solubility property.
