rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the physical-state property.

written.text: How does boiling point of liquid depend upon the nature of liquid and intermolecular forces.
modelAnswer: The boiling point depends on the nature of the liquid, because its molecular structure and polarity affect the attractions between its particles.
During boiling, energy must be supplied to overcome the intermolecular forces and separate the molecules.
A liquid with stronger intermolecular forces needs more energy to boil and therefore has a higher boiling point.
A liquid with weaker intermolecular forces needs less energy and has a lower boiling point.
written.followUp: Explain how stronger intermolecular forces affect the boiling point of a liquid.

rubric.why: The nature and structure of a liquid determine the attractions between its particles.
rubric.description: States that boiling point depends on the nature or molecular structure of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating boiling point to the nature, structure, or polarity of the liquid.

rubric.why: Identifies intermolecular attraction as the relevant force to overcome during boiling.
rubric.description: Identifies intermolecular forces between liquid particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning intermolecular forces or attractions between molecules.

rubric.why: Boiling requires enough energy to overcome attractions between particles.
rubric.description: Explains that energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking boiling to overcoming the attractions.

rubric.why: The strength of attraction determines the relative boiling point.
rubric.description: States that stronger forces give a higher boiling point and weaker forces give a lower boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between force strength and boiling point.

written.text: Differentiate between physical and chemical properties.
modelAnswer: A physical property can be observed or measured without changing the chemical composition or identity of a substance.
A chemical property describes how a substance can react to form new substances, changing its chemical composition.

written.text: When does an electron emit or absorb energy?
modelAnswer: An electron emits energy when it moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level.
An electron absorbs energy when it moves from a lower energy level to a higher energy level.
written.followUp: What happens to an electron when it moves from a higher energy level to a lower one?

rubric.description: States that an electron emits energy when it moves from a higher energy level to a lower one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying emission during a downward transition.

rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy when it moves from a lower energy level to a higher one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying absorption during an upward transition.

written.text: What do you know about Dobereiner's triads?
modelAnswer: Dobereiner arranged some elements in groups of three, called triads, whose elements had similar chemical properties.
The atomic mass of the middle element was approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements.
For example, Li, Na and K form a triad.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the middle element’s atomic mass as approximately the arithmetic mean of the other two.

written.text: Why atomic radius increases down the group in the periodic table?
modelAnswer: Down a group, each successive element has an additional occupied electron shell.
Therefore, the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and the atomic radius increases.

rubric.description: The outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus, so atomic radius increases
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus and the atomic radius consequently increases.

written.text: Write two properties of solution.

written.text: How many isotopes of hydrogen are there? How they are used in power generation?
modelAnswer: Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (¹₁H), deuterium (²₁H) and tritium (³₁H).
Deuterium and tritium can be used as fuels for nuclear fusion to generate power.
²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + energy
The fusion reaction produces helium and a neutron and releases a large amount of energy.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming or identifying all three isotopes.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share electrons.

written.text: Explain how are dilute solution prepared from concentrated solutions?
modelAnswer: Use the dilution formula M1V1 = M2V2 to calculate the volume of concentrated solution required.
Put some distilled water into a volumetric flask.
Measure the calculated volume of concentrated solution with a pipette and transfer it to the flask.
Add distilled water until the bottom of the meniscus reaches the calibration mark.
Stopper the flask and mix the solution thoroughly.
When diluting an acid, add the acid slowly to water, never water to acid.

written.text: Why does ice floats on water?
modelAnswer: Ice floats on water because it is less dense than liquid water.
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open structure in ice, so the molecules are farther apart and the same mass occupies more volume.

written.text: What is effusion? Explain with an example.
modelAnswer: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum or a region of lower pressure.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, helium (He).
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, hydrogen (H₂).
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, water (H₂O).
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, phosphorus (P₄).

written.text: Draw a labelled diagram to show the presence of protons in the discharge tube and explain how were canal rays produced?
modelAnswer: Diagram (not to scale):
[Anode (+)]   → positive canal rays →   [perforated cathode (−), with holes]
low-pressure gas in a glass discharge tube; high voltage applied across the electrodes
The tube contains gas at low pressure and a high voltage is applied across its electrodes.
The discharge ionises the gas atoms, producing positively charged particles and electrons.
The positive particles move towards the cathode and pass through its perforations, forming canal rays.
When the gas is hydrogen, the positive particles are H⁺ ions (protons).

written.text: Why does the size of atoms decrease in a period from left to right?
modelAnswer: From left to right across a period, the nuclear charge increases.
The added electrons enter the same shell, so the stronger attraction between the nucleus and the electrons pulls them closer.

rubric.how: Award for linking the same shell and stronger nuclear attraction to the decrease in size.

written.text: Why does sodium form a chemical bond with chlorine?
modelAnswer: A sodium atom loses one electron to form a positively charged sodium ion, Na⁺.

written.text: What is the difference between Rutherford’s Atomic Theory and Neil Bohr’s Atomic Theory?

Rutherford’s theory did not explain the stability of the atom.
Bohr proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus only in fixed orbits, or energy levels, each having a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while in a fixed orbit; they absorb or emit energy when they move between energy levels.

written.text: Write down any four Properties of Metals.
modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous, meaning they have a shiny surface.
Metals are malleable and can be hammered into sheets.
Metals are ductile and can be drawn into wires.
Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity.

written.text: Define Avogadro’s number. Write down one example.
modelAnswer: Avogadro’s number is the number of particles present in one mole of a substance: 6.02 × 10^23 particles mol−1.
For example, 1 mol of water contains 6.02 × 10^23 water molecules.
written.followUp: Define a mole and state how many molecules are present in 2 mol of CO2.

rubric.why: An example applies the number to a specific mole quantity of a substance.
rubric.description: Gives one valid example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example correctly relating one mole to Avogadro’s number of particles.

written.text: How does electron differ from neutron?
modelAnswer: An electron has a charge of −1, while a neutron has no charge (0).
An electron has a very small mass, about 1/1836 u; a neutron has a mass of about 1 u.
written.followUp: Compare a proton and an electron by charge and relative mass.

rubric.why: A neutron has a mass of about 1 u, while an electron is much lighter.
rubric.description: Compares the relative masses of an electron and neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly distinguishing their masses.

written.text: Write down two observations made by Rutherford’s atomic model
modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.

rubric.description: A small number were deflected; a very small number bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing deflection or backward scattering of a small number of alpha particles.

written.text: What do you know about Mendeleev?
modelAnswer: Dmitri Mendeleev was a Russian chemist.
He arranged the elements in a periodic table in order of increasing atomic masses.

written.text: Where f-block is present in the Periodic table?
modelAnswer: The f-block is shown as two separate rows at the bottom of the periodic table.
These rows are the lanthanide and actinide series.

written.text: Write the name and symbols of Group I elements.
modelAnswer: Hydrogen (H), lithium (Li), sodium (Na), and potassium (K) are Group I elements.
Rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs), and francium (Fr) are also Group I elements.

written.text: Define electron affinity. Give one example.
modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when an isolated gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
For example: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ + energy.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example showing an atom gaining an electron to form a negative ion.

written.text: Write down four types of chemical bond.
modelAnswer: The four types of chemical bond are ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent, and metallic bonds.

written.text: Point out the type of covalent bond in the following molecules. (i) C₂H₂ (ii) CH₄
modelAnswer: C₂H₂: the two carbon atoms are joined by a triple covalent bond.

written.text: Why do the ionic compounds have high melting and boiling point?
modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
A large amount of energy is required to overcome these forces, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.
written.followUp: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?

rubric.why: Explains that oppositely charged ions in an ionic compound are held together by strong electrostatic forces.
rubric.description: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction act between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Connects the strong ionic attractions to the large energy needed to separate ions.
rubric.description: A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that substantial energy is required to overcome the ionic attractions.

written.text: Why amorphous solids do not have sharp melting points?
modelAnswer: Amorphous solids have an irregular arrangement of particles.
Different parts soften gradually over a range of temperatures, so they do not have a sharp melting point.
written.followUp: Why do crystalline solids have a definite melting point?

rubric.why: Amorphous solids lack the regular, orderly arrangement of particles found in crystals.

rubric.why: Different parts of an amorphous solid soften or melt at different temperatures, rather than at one fixed temperature.
rubric.description: Explains that amorphous solids soften over a range of temperatures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they soften or melt over a temperature range rather than at a sharp melting point.

written.text: Define solubility. In which solvent paints are soluble?
modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature to form a saturated solution.
Paints are soluble in turpentine oil.

rubric.why: Turpentine is a solvent used to dissolve many paints.
rubric.description: Names turpentine oil as a solvent for paints.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for turpentine or turpentine oil.

written.text: Define suspension. Give example.
modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which insoluble solid particles are dispersed in a liquid and may settle on standing.
Muddy water is an example of a suspension.

rubric.why: A suspension contains undissolved particles dispersed in another substance.

rubric.why: Muddy water and chalk in water are common examples of suspensions.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of a suspension.

written.text: Name any two moderately reactive metals.
modelAnswer: Zinc is a moderately reactive metal.

rubric.why: Silver is lustrous and is also malleable, ductile, or a good conductor of heat and electricity.
rubric.description: Gives one correct characteristic of silver.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one characteristic such as lustre, malleability, ductility, or good conductivity.

rubric.why: Any two distinct correct characteristics satisfy the question.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct characteristic of silver.

written.text: How non metals play essential role in the safety of life?
modelAnswer: Ozone, an allotrope of oxygen, absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
This protects living organisms from the harmful effects of that radiation.
written.followUp: How does the ozone layer help protect living organisms?

rubric.why: Ozone in the atmosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

rubric.why: By absorbing UV radiation, ozone helps protect living things from its harmful effects.

written.text: Write down postulates of Bohr’s atomic theory.
modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits, called shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
An electron absorbs energy to move from a lower-energy orbit to a higher-energy orbit.
It emits energy when it moves from a higher-energy orbit to a lower-energy orbit.
written.followUp: State Bohr’s postulates about electron shells and explain what happens when an electron moves between shells.

rubric.why: Checks the postulate describing electron paths.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits or shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying fixed electron paths around the nucleus.

rubric.why: Checks the energy associated with a permitted orbit.
rubric.description: States that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that permitted orbits have definite energy.

rubric.why: Checks the stability of electrons in permitted orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that there is no energy loss in a stationary orbit.

rubric.why: Checks the energy changes during transitions between orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower-energy orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each correct direction of energy transfer; award 2 marks for both.

written.text: Explain, how is evaporation affected by different factors.
modelAnswer: Higher temperature increases evaporation because more particles have enough energy to escape from the liquid.
A larger exposed surface area increases evaporation because more liquid particles can escape at the same time.
Higher humidity slows evaporation; low humidity makes evaporation faster.
Greater wind speed increases evaporation by carrying water vapour away from the liquid surface.
written.followUp: Explain how temperature, surface area, humidity and wind speed affect the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of temperature.
rubric.description: Explains that higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of temperature.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of exposed surface area.
rubric.description: Explains that a larger exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of surface area.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of humidity.
rubric.description: Explains that higher humidity slows evaporation, while lower humidity makes it faster.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between humidity and evaporation.

rubric.why: Checks the effect of moving air.
rubric.description: Explains that greater wind speed increases evaporation by carrying vapour away from the surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of wind speed.

written.text: How does homogeneous mixture differ from heterogeneous mixture? Give example.
modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; its components are evenly mixed, as in salt solution.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, as in a mixture of sand and water.

rubric.why: Checks the contrast and example of a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: States that a heterogeneous mixture has non-uniform composition and gives a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature and an example such as sand and water.

written.text: Which isotopes are used as tracers in medicines?
modelAnswer: Iodine-131 is used as a tracer to examine the thyroid gland.
Sodium-24 is used as a tracer to study blood circulation.

rubric.why: Checks identification of a medical tracer isotope.

written.text: What are the trends of shielding effect in periodic table?
modelAnswer: Shielding effect increases down a group because each step adds an occupied electron shell.
Shielding effect remains nearly constant across a period because the number of inner shells does not change.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct down-group trend.

rubric.why: Checks the trend across a period.
rubric.description: States that shielding effect remains nearly constant across a period because electrons are added to the same main shell and the number of inner shells is unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct across-period trend.

written.text: What is Octat rule?
modelAnswer: The octet rule states that atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to have eight electrons in their outermost shell.
This gives them a stable electronic configuration.

written.text: Describe at least two necessary conditions for formation of a covalent bond.
modelAnswer: The combining atoms must have unpaired electrons in their outer shells.
Their half-filled orbitals must overlap, and the electrons forming the bond must have opposite spins.

written.text: What is absolute zero temperature? What is its value in degree Celsius.

written.text: What are amorphous solids? Give examples.
modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose particles are not arranged in a regular, orderly pattern.

written.text: What is vapour pressure? How different factors affect on it?
modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour when it is in equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container.
As temperature increases, vapour pressure increases.
More volatile liquids, which have weaker intermolecular attractions, have higher vapour pressure.
At a fixed temperature, surface area does not affect equilibrium vapour pressure; it only changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached.

written.text: How are free radicals formed?
modelAnswer: Free radicals are formed by the homolytic fission of a covalent bond.

written.text: How ionization energy of sodium is less than that of magnesium?
modelAnswer: Sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, while magnesium has 2,8,2.

written.text: Justify HCl molecule is a polar molecule.
modelAnswer: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electron pair in HCl is attracted more towards chlorine.

written.text: Define diffusion of gases with an example.
modelAnswer: Diffusion of gases is the spreading and mixing of gas particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

written.text: Why solids are denser than liquids?

written.text: Give five differences between Rutherford's atomic theory and Bohr's atomic theory.
modelAnswer: 1. Rutherford proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in any orbit; Bohr proposed that electrons occupy only certain fixed orbits or energy levels.
2. Rutherford’s model did not assign fixed energies to electron orbits; Bohr’s model assigned a definite energy to each allowed orbit.
3. Rutherford’s model could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus; Bohr’s model explained atomic stability through stable orbits.
4. In Rutherford’s model, an accelerating electron should continuously radiate energy; in Bohr’s model, an electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate energy.
5. Rutherford’s model did not explain the line spectra of atoms; Bohr explained them by absorption or emission of energy when electrons jump between energy levels.
written.followUp: Give five differences between Rutherford’s atomic model and Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford allowed electrons to move in any orbit, while Bohr proposed only certain fixed orbits.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting Rutherford’s any-orbit model with Bohr’s fixed orbits.

rubric.why: Bohr assigned a definite energy to each permitted orbit, unlike Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Compares the energy of the orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Bohr’s allowed orbits have definite energies, unlike Rutherford’s model.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability, whereas Bohr described stable orbits.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model implied continuous radiation by revolving electrons; Bohr proposed that electrons do not radiate energy in permitted orbits.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting continuous radiation in Rutherford’s model with no radiation in Bohr’s permitted orbits.

rubric.why: Bohr explained line spectra by electron transitions between energy levels; Rutherford’s model did not explain them.
rubric.description: Compares the explanation of atomic line spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting Bohr’s explanation of line spectra with electron transitions between energy levels.

written.text: Define evaporation. Describe various factors affecting it.
modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface at a temperature below its boiling point.
Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation because more particles have enough energy to escape.
A larger surface area increases the rate because more particles are exposed at the surface.
Higher wind speed increases evaporation by carrying vapour away; low humidity also increases evaporation because the air can take up more vapour.

written.text: Differentiate between unsaturated solution and super saturated solution using example of sodium thiosulphate (Na₂S₂O₃).
modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than the maximum amount that can dissolve at a given temperature, so it can dissolve more sodium thiosulphate at that temperature.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution normally holds at the same temperature.
For example, an unsaturated sodium thiosulphate solution can dissolve more solute.
A hot saturated sodium thiosulphate solution, cooled carefully without crystallisation, becomes supersaturated; it may crystallise if disturbed or seeded.

written.text: How does a Coordinate covalent bond form? Explain with examples.
modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond forms when one atom donates both electrons of a shared pair to another atom or ion.
The donating atom has a lone pair, and the acceptor has a vacant orbital.
For example, NH3 donates a lone pair to H+ to form NH4+: NH3 + H+ → NH4+.
Similarly, H2O donates a lone pair to H+ to form H3O+: H2O + H+ → H3O+.

written.text: Compare both Rutherford's and Bohr's atomic theories.

Bohr proposed that electrons move in fixed orbits, each with a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy in these stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when they move between orbits, explaining the hydrogen spectrum.

written.text: Define a covalent bond and explain its various types.
modelAnswer: A covalent bond is a chemical bond formed between atoms by sharing one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons; for example, N₂.

written.text: Describe Rutherford’s atomic model with the help of a diagram.
modelAnswer: Rutherford’s atomic model has the following features:
An atom has a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre.
Almost all the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular paths; the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and electrons holds them in the atom.
Most of the volume of an atom is empty space.
Diagram:
e⁻
e⁻ (  [ + nucleus ]  ) e⁻
e⁻
The nucleus is at the centre, electrons are around it, and the space between them is mostly empty.

rubric.description: Describes the nucleus as very small, dense and positively charged, with most of the atomic mass concentrated in it.

written.text: Explain any four characteristics of a colloid.
modelAnswer: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture, although it may appear homogeneous to the naked eye.
Its particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
Colloidal particles scatter light, producing the Tyndall effect.
The particles show continuous, random Brownian movement.

written.text: Define molecular formula with an example.
modelAnswer: A molecular formula shows the kinds and actual numbers of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a substance.
For example, H₂O shows that one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

written.text: Write down electronic configuration of magnesium.
modelAnswer: Magnesium has atomic number 12, so a neutral magnesium atom has 12 electrons.
Its electronic configuration in shells is 2, 8, 2.
Magnesium has two electrons in its outermost shell.
written.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of calcium (atomic number 20) in shells.

written.text: Why in any element, atomic number is more fundamental property than atomic mass?
modelAnswer: The atomic number is more fundamental than atomic mass because it gives the number of protons in an atom and therefore determines the identity of the element.
It also determines the electronic configuration and hence the chemical properties of the element.
Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different atomic masses.

rubric.description: Links atomic number with the proton number and element identity.

rubric.description: Explains why atomic number is more fundamental than atomic mass.
rubric.how: Award for linking atomic number to electronic configuration and chemical properties, or for explaining that isotopes have the same atomic number but different masses.

written.text: Differentiate between group and period of periodic table.
modelAnswer: A group is a vertical column in the periodic table; its elements have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.
A period is a horizontal row; its elements have the same number of electron shells.

written.text: Why does ionization energy increase in a period from left to right and decrease down a group?
modelAnswer: Across a period, effective nuclear charge increases while the outer electrons remain in the same shell, so attraction to the nucleus increases and more energy is needed to remove an electron.
Down a group, additional shells increase the distance and shielding of the outer electron, so the nuclear attraction decreases and less energy is needed to remove it.
written.followUp: Explain why ionization energy increases from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Links the increased nuclear attraction across a period to the energy required to remove an electron.
rubric.description: Explains the increase in ionization energy across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that effective nuclear charge increases while the outer electrons remain in the same shell, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that additional shells increase the distance and shielding of the outer electron, decreasing nuclear attraction and the energy needed to remove it.

written.text: Define the term “boiling point”. Give an example.
modelAnswer: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into gas throughout the liquid.
For example, water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm pressure.

written.text: Write down two causes of allotropy.
modelAnswer: Allotropy may be caused by different numbers of atoms in the molecules of an element.

written.text: What is an alloy?
modelAnswer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a non-metal.

written.text: Which one of the following solutions is more concentrated: one molar or three molar
modelAnswer: The three-molar (3 M) solution is more concentrated.

written.text: What is a molecule? Describe any four types of molecules with examples.
modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, helium (He).
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, oxygen (O₂).
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, ozone (O₃).
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, phosphorus (P₄).

written.text: Define Quantum. Write down the difference between Rutherford Atomic Theory and Bohr’s Atomic Theory.
modelAnswer: A quantum is a fixed, discrete packet of energy that an atom can absorb or emit.
Rutherford proposed that electrons revolve around a small, positively charged nucleus.
According to Rutherford’s model, revolving electrons should continuously lose energy and fall into the nucleus; therefore, it could not explain atomic stability.
Bohr proposed that electrons occupy only certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus.
Electrons do not radiate energy while in these stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when they move between energy levels.
written.followUp: State one limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model and explain how Bohr’s model addressed it.

rubric.description: Defines a quantum as a discrete packet or fixed amount of energy.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed, non-radiating energy levels and 1 mark for absorption or emission of energy during transitions.

written.text: What is meant by “like dissolves like”? Explain it with examples.
modelAnswer: “Like dissolves like” means that a solute dissolves best in a solvent with a similar nature or polarity.
Polar solutes generally dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar solutes generally dissolve in non-polar solvents, because their intermolecular attractions are similar.
For example, ionic sodium chloride and polar sugar dissolve in polar water.
Non-polar oil dissolves in non-polar petrol; oil does not dissolve in polar water.

written.text: How many molecules are present in 1.5 g H₂O?
modelAnswer: Given: m = 1.5 g = 1.5 × 10⁻³ kg; M(H₂O) = 18 g mol⁻¹ = 18 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = m/M; N = nNₐ.
Substitution: n = (1.5 × 10⁻³ kg)/(18 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹) = 0.0833 mol.
N = 0.0833 mol × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 5.02 × 10²² molecules.

written.text: Why is breaking of a bond an endothermic process?

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid contrast or example. Note that some carbon-containing substances, such as carbon dioxide and carbonates, are inorganic.

written.text: How are organic compounds useful for us?
modelAnswer: Organic compounds are used as food and as fuels such as petrol and natural gas.
They are also used to make medicines, clothing fibres and plastics.
written.followUp: Name four everyday uses of organic compounds.

rubric.why: Food and fuels are important uses of organic compounds.
rubric.description: Identifies organic compounds as food or fuels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming food or fuel as a use.

rubric.why: Organic compounds are used to make a range of useful products.
rubric.description: Names a product made from organic compounds, such as medicines, clothing fibres or plastics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least one valid product use.

written.text: What does happen when naphtha is heated?
modelAnswer: When naphtha is strongly heated, its larger hydrocarbon molecules break into smaller hydrocarbons; this process is called cracking.
The products include petrol and smaller hydrocarbons such as alkenes and gases.
written.followUp: What is cracking of petroleum fractions? Name one product formed from naphtha by cracking.

rubric.why: Award for explaining what happens to the larger hydrocarbon molecules.
rubric.description: States that heating naphtha breaks larger hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the heating and breakdown into smaller hydrocarbons.

rubric.why: Award for naming a valid product of cracking.
rubric.description: Names a product such as petrol, an alkene or a hydrocarbon gas.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for at least one valid product.

written.text: Write differences between elements, compounds and mixtures?
modelAnswer: An element consists of only one kind of atom; a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined; a mixture contains substances physically mixed together.
The elements in a compound are present in a fixed proportion, whereas the components of a mixture may be present in any proportion.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements, while the components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical means, whereas a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
written.followUp: Compare elements, compounds and mixtures by their composition and method of separation.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing the basic composition of all three types of matter.
rubric.description: Identifies an element as one kind of atom, a compound as chemically combined elements, and a mixture as physically combined substances.
rubric.how: Give 2 marks when all three distinctions are stated; give 1 mark if two are correct.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing the fixed composition of compounds from mixtures.
rubric.description: States that compounds have a fixed ratio of elements, whereas mixture components can be in any proportion.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both parts of the comparison.

rubric.why: Award for comparing the properties of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.description: States that a compound has properties different from its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both parts of the comparison.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing how compounds and mixtures can be separated.
rubric.description: States that compounds are separated chemically, while mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for both methods of separation.

written.text: Explain Bohr’s atomic model.
modelAnswer: An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons move around it.
Electrons can move only in certain fixed orbits, or shells, each having a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in one of these permitted orbits.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it falls to a lower-energy orbit.
written.followUp: State Bohr’s postulates about electron shells and the emission or absorption of energy.

rubric.why: This identifies the atom’s central structure and the particles around it.
rubric.description: States that an atom has a central nucleus with electrons around it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both the nucleus and electrons.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model allows electrons to occupy only particular orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: States that electrons occupy fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed orbits, shells or definite energy levels.

rubric.why: Electrons in permitted stationary orbits do not lose energy by radiation.
rubric.description: States that an electron does not radiate energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

rubric.why: An electron changes energy when it moves between permitted orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit or emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing either transition with its energy change.

written.text:
Explain the variation in the following properties in the periods giving reasons.
i- Atomic radius      ii- Ionization energy
modelAnswer: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius decreases.
The nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same main shell, so the stronger attraction pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.
Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
The outer electrons are held more strongly because of the increased nuclear attraction and smaller atomic radius, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.
written.followUp: Explain how atomic radius and ionization energy change from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Atomic radius becomes smaller across a period.
rubric.description: States that atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons in the same main shell more strongly.
rubric.description: Explains the decrease in radius by increasing nuclear charge while electrons are added to the same shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased nuclear charge and the same shell to the smaller radius.

rubric.why: Ionization energy generally rises across a period.
rubric.description: States that ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Stronger attraction makes the outer electron harder to remove, so more energy is required; both the cause and consequence are needed for these marks.
rubric.description: Links the stronger attraction on outer electrons to the increased energy needed to remove one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the stronger nuclear attraction and 1 mark for stating that more energy is needed to remove an electron.

written.text: Describe harmful effects of the major pollutants present in the air.
modelAnswer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the blood, reducing its ability to carry oxygen and causing serious health effects.
Sulphur dioxide irritates the respiratory system and can contribute to acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides can cause respiratory problems and contribute to acid rain and photochemical smog; particulate matter can damage the lungs.
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) damage the ozone layer, while hydrocarbons can contribute to photochemical smog.
written.followUp: Describe two harmful effects each of carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide in air.

rubric.why: Award for a correct health effect of carbon monoxide.
rubric.description: States that carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin and reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying ability.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for linking carbon monoxide to haemoglobin or reduced oxygen transport.

rubric.why: Award for a correct harmful effect of sulphur dioxide.
rubric.description: States that sulphur dioxide harms the respiratory system or contributes to acid rain.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for one valid effect of sulphur dioxide.

rubric.why: Award for describing the harmful effects of other major air pollutants.
rubric.description: Names nitrogen oxides or particulate pollution and gives a valid effect, such as acid rain, smog or lung harm.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for a pollutant-effect pair.

rubric.why: Award for identifying another major pollutant and its environmental harm.
rubric.description: States that CFCs damage the ozone layer or that hydrocarbons contribute to photochemical smog.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for a correct pollutant-effect pair.
